Gasly takes shock Italian GP pole and denies Russell

📅 05 Sep 2026 | ⏱️ 16 min read (3288 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Co

⏱️ ~16 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that sometimes inspiration can come from the unlikeliest of sources.
  • It turned out Gasly and Russell had been playing online chess until about 15 minutes before qualifying.
  • Industry observers note that “Since the [drivers’] briefing last night, I figured out that he [Russell] is obsessed with chess, and so am I,” Gasly explained later in his press conference.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that sometimes inspiration can come from the unlikeliest of sources. After claiming the first pole of his Formula One career, an absolutely stunning effort in his 192nd attempt – edging out Mercedes’ George Russell right at the death – Alpine’s Pierre Gasly revealed that a harmless jibe from his performance coach Ben Thorpe just before the session started had riled him up.

It turned out Gasly and Russell had been playing online chess until about 15 minutes before qualifying.

Industry observers note that “Since the [drivers’] briefing last night, I figured out that he [Russell] is obsessed with chess, and so am I,” Gasly explained later in his press conference. “There are a few of us in the paddock who are. So we have exchanged our IDs on Chess.com and we have had a little game going on.

Industry observers note that “I won yesterday, and another one that carried on into today,” the Frenchman added. “I was feeling confident and I was picking [taking] piece after piece. Then Ben told me: ‘You are getting George here but he is going to get you in a few minutes!’. And I thought ‘F--- off!’.”.

Sources indicate that what a way to break your duck. And what a day on which to do it. On Friday, Gasly lost his only podium of the season when the International Court of Appeal reinstated two five-second penalties he received in Monaco, dropping him from third to seventh in that race. The ruling produced fireworks when Flavio Briatore, Alpine’s executive adviser, then accused one of the judges on the ICA panel of being biased towards McLaren, one of two teams who had brought the appeal.

Another 24 hours later, the fireworks were for all the right reasons. And there was no appealing the result; the start of Russell’s final lap in Q3 was slightly compromised by Red Bull’s Max Verstappen, but the Englishman could have no real complaints, losing out by 0.060secs in the end, prompting wild celebrations in the Alpine garage.

To say the result was a surprise would be an understatement. This was the Enstone team’s first pole in 17 years, since Fernando Alonso took P1 Renault at the 2009 Hungarian Grand Prix.

It has been revealed that the warning signs were there. Alpine had been quick all weekend. But the Tifosi packing Monza’s grandstands fully expected it to be a battle between Mercedes and their beloved Ferrari for pole.

It has been revealed that the Scuderia’s performance was underwhelming. Charles Leclerc and Lewis Hamilton were only ninth and 10th quickest in Q2, the latter squeaking into Q3 by one thousandth of a second from Audi’s Gabriel Bortoleto. “F--- me,” Hamilton said after dodging that bullet.

And although they improved a bit in Q3, Hamilton managing to claim P5, just behind Leclerc in P4, they never threatened the front row. In fact, they later got lucky as McLaren’s Oscar Piastri, who took P3, was later hit with a three-place grid drop post-qualifying for impeding Liam Lawson, meaning both Ferrari drivers rose one place.

It has been revealed that it could prove significant. Hamilton, like Russell, knows this weekend represents a golden opportunity to close the gap to Kimi Antonelli in the title race. The two Britons are tied second in the championship heading into the weekend, 59 points behind the Italian. But Antonelli, who sacrificed his qualifying to help Russell, must start from the back of the grid on Sunday due to exceeding the permitted number of engines in a season.

It promises to be a fascinating race, with Antonelli fighting his way through the pack and Russell and Hamilton trying to make hay while they can. Russell sounded confident. “I think they [Alpine] have got a car that’s got some good straight-line speed, which will be nice for them in the race. But, yeah, confident I’ve got the pace to go for the win.”.

Recent findings suggest that could he be underestimating Gasly again? The Frenchman, who lives locally in Milan and speaks fluent Italian, has won here before. He claimed the only victory of his F1 career at Monza for AlphaTauri in 2020.

“Anything is possible tomorrow,” insisted Steve Nielsen, Alpine’s managing director. “We didn’t expect to be in pole position, we are. Tomorrow, good starts, good strategy, good pit stops – who knows? Let’s try to win it.”.

Sources indicate that gasly himself said he had no idea what he was capable of. “My strategy is to stay first as long as I can. How long is that going to be? I have no idea. My focus is going to be on my driving and making no mistakes and making the best out of what I have.” Perhaps that will be enough for another checkmate.

Antonelli acknowledged that his engine-parts grid penalty meant he had no reason not to assist his teamate Russell by offering towing assistance.

According to recent reports, he seemed a little peeved at times on the radio, but he did his job. With Russell likely to need to return the favour for him later this season, there is no point causing bother.

According to recent reports, he told Sky Sports: “It’s what I have to do. The team asked me and of course I did what I had to do, I tried to help as much as possible. It’s a bit weird going in two, even the lap I did alone was a bit of a weird feeling. Overall with the penalty today I had to be a good teammate and I had to help as much as I could. I think I did a good job with that and happy it worked out.”.

Here’s Oscar Piastri, asked if a pole had been possible: “I don’t think so, no. I think the first lap felt good and I tried to see if anyone wanted to go in front out of the pit lane but no one did and I knew it was always going to be difficult and misjudged the braking a little bit and locked up. That was the session but good to have a decent result, it has been a while. I’ll take it.”.

According to recent reports, alpine managing director Steve Nielsen noted to Sky Sports that they were aiming high: “Pierre is a class act, as you say, if you give him the machine, he will deliver. We failed to do that a few times last year. We haven’t always given him the most competitive machinery this year, but when we have he has delivered. Particularly earlier in the season so to see the team bounce back, to see him deliver on the track he knows well, he lives locally, he lives in Milan. It was wonderful.

In a recent development, “We mustn’t forget Franco either, he’s done a great job today. I really feel we have given them a good car, and who knows? Anything is possible tomorrow.”.

In a recent development, here’s what he said immediately after the session: “Massive congrats to Pierre because that’s an incredible performance. We were actually playing a game of chess about 15 minutes before qualifying and he beat me there and I thought ‘well I think I’ll beat you in qualifying’ and here we are - he’s ahead of me again! I was disappointed not to get pole. It was a bit messy with Verstappen opening the lap. But Pierre and Alpine have been super fast, even from Q1. Happy to see them get a good result.”.

Gasly’s advantage, it appears, seems to be over Russell’s car understeering and lacking grip in turbulent air.

P1 ☝️#F1 #ItalianGP pic.twitter.com/U0hebWsjWY.

He says: “It was amazing, thank you everyone. It was an incredible qualy. I felt very good in the car. I was trying to chip away in evert session. I’m so happy, it’s been nine years trying to get a pole. First win [was] in Monza, to get pole is very special.”.

He then pays credit to his team and the fans in Italian, and I am leaning on my Latin to get the gist of it.

“I was disappointed not to get the pole,” admits Russell who said he had been playing chess with Gasly before the game and the Frenchman won that, with Russell confident he was going to beat him in qualifying.

According to recent reports, alpine been in the news all weekend. Fair to say that pole lap from Gasly is better PR for the team than Flavio Briatore’s bizarre outburst in the FIA press conference yesterday. Well done that man.

Recent findings suggest that his tone is evidently disappointed. In truth, given Hamilton is fifth, he is in a strong position to have the best of the weekend.

Gasly, yes, was fastest, but Russell has been the most consistent.

Piastri could be in trouble, too, for impeding earlier in the day’s sesion. Ferrari, in fourth and fifth, do not look entirely competitive.

Russell is second, Piastri third, Leclerc fourth, Hamilton fifth, Verstappen sixth, Antonelli seventh, Colapinto eighth, Norris ninth and Lindblad 10th.

He starts his flying lap, and locks up at turn 1 and exceeds track limits. That means Norris will be unable to get a tow from him too.

After being the quickest at FP2 and FP3, he is top of the pack once more with a bit over five minutes left.

Antonelli has done him a favour there, but Russell may need to return the favour in similar circumstances down the line.

Hamilton is now down in ninth, and struggling, about 0.8s off the pace.

Piastri may be in for some bother.

Hamilton needs to catch Leclerc to get a tow. It failed to happen last time out.

Piastri finished Q2 in P2 but it looks likely he'll be penalised for this incident involving Lawson#F1 #ItalianGP pic.twitter.com/RGzzEeqyql.

Lawson, Hulkenberg, Sainz, Ocon, Bearman and Bortoleto are all out.

Hamilton is 10th, one-thousandth of a second quick enough to scrape through, and Leclrec ninth.

“**** me” exclaims Hamilton, without saying, ‘Asterisk’ once.

Antonelli asks for the chance to go out with another team ahead so he can get a tow of his own.

Norris now second quickest, so perhaps those brakes are up to speed.

There is some suggestion that Hamilton might need a front wing change.

The Silver Arrows working in tandem Kimi in front, George slipstreaming behind #F1 #ItalianGP pic.twitter.com/H476E91GJs.

But Gasly is going fastest in his out lap.

Verstappen now goes fastest. Lawson is in behind, with Carlos Sainz making a surprise appearance up top.

Hamilton and Russell are yet to lay down times.

Norris is uncomfortable with his brakes at Monza.

Given he’s well outside of the fastest for now, the pressure is on him to make Q3.

The two Aston Martins are out, along with Yuki Tsunoda, Alex Albon, Valtteri Bottas and Sergio Perez.

Q2 awaits, with Gasly fastest - aiming for what would be his first pole.

According to recent reports, alonso, meanwhile, has wirthdrawn from the session. Things going wrong for the veteran, who must have no other hobbies.

FOUR MINUTES TO GO IN Q1TOP 6 ⬆️Gasly VerstappenColapintoAntonelliRussellHamiltonBOTTOM 6 ⬇️Hulkenberg AlbonBottasAlonsoStrollPerez#F1 #ItalianGP pic.twitter.com/BYdYjrjtnu.

Pierre Gasly takes his Alpine for a spin. He is now fastest, with Verstappen second, and Colapinto bookending the Dutchman.

Antonelli and then Russell next, with the stricken Antonelli likely to give his colleague a tow.

The Red Bull man is 0.216s clear of Hamilton, with Piastri just behind.

No surprising stragglers just yet, but 11 minutes to go of this section.

We’ve 16 minutes left, and some cars are finally coming out to do battle.

18 minutes ahead before the final two rounds. Nobody is doing anything. As they say in football: tactically fascinating.

In a recent development, monza paddock is absolutely sweltering. 33.8C out here. I just passed Fabio Capello on my way back to the media centre. He was speaking to Sky Sports Italia so I wasn’t able to give him my thoughts on where he went wrong at the 2010 World Cup.

Industry observers note that decent ding dong between Hamilton and Verstappen in practice earlier. Hopefully Hamilton is fired up for this. With Antonelli taking his grid drop at his home race, there’s a massive opportunity for both Hamilton and Russell to close the gap this weekend.

The tifosi are ready 🙌It's time for qualifying at the Temple of Speed 👊#F1 #ItalianGP pic.twitter.com/jeiTcb8Ij2.

The cars will soon be out on the track, and we’ll have reports of their progress.

There are actually times when affection for a car firm makes sense, despite what I mentioned earlier.

According to recent reports, sound on... listen to the reception for Charles and Lewis ❤️#F1 #ItalianGP @ScuderiaFerrari pic.twitter.com/kk6BvA1UdC.

As touched on earlier, Lewis Hamilton has to hope Charles Leclerc will work with him.

Recent findings suggest that the Monegasque (look it up) is the junior partner at this point, whether he wants to be or not. That might not make him entirely delighted, but he can tow the British driver around and give him a launch for fast laps, if he’s feeling helpful.

Everyone now has access to PowerPoint, which means we all now have to have, “learnings.”.

Imagine if someone you met in real life said that to you.

3 hours of laps and learnings done.#ItalianGP pic.twitter.com/GTvOvL5L5M.

Given Antonelli is still one of the quickest on the track, it would be no surprise if he can at least make the top 10.

Favourable accidents and yellow flags might offer up more opportunities, too, but both Hamilton and Russell need to strike while they have such a clear advantage.

George Russell tops Lewis Hamilton in final practice in Monza 🇮🇹💪 pic.twitter.com/jxIO13aRX6.

I’m as massive a fan of F1 as the next man, assuming the next man quite likes F1, but there is something strange about supporting a car company, isn’t there?

It has been revealed that 🇮🇹 Sentendo il calore dell'Italia! 🥰🇬🇧 Feeling the warmth of Italy! 🥰 pic.twitter.com/ze6Ww1Z0zx.

The session starts in around 40 minutes, so drivers are on their Gameboys and Instagram, and reading the weekend edition of The Telegraph.

Words we live by, this weekend and always ❤️ pic.twitter.com/0QoGlpzOHI.

Here’s our interview with Alex Albon about a grim weekend at Monza.

Industry observers note that “Alex Albon remembers the 2022 Italian Grand Prix well. He had been looking forward to it. ‘We had a car which was good down the straights that year so I was quite excited to be going to Monza,” the Williams driver recalls, a little wistfully.

‘We did FP1 and FP2 and sure enough we were quick so I was like: ‘This is going to be a good weekend.’.

“Albon could not have been more wrong. He remembers waking at around 1am that night and being unable to get back to sleep.

According to recent reports, “What happened next was the stuff of nightmares. Albon called the doctor, was diagnosed with appendicitis, sent to San Gerardo Hospital in Monza for surgery, only to suffer an unexpected complication during the procedure, which resulted in acute respiratory failure.”.

He shares the joint record with Michael Schumacher for most wins at Monza.

Industry observers note that schumacher, a Ferrari legend, ended his career with five. Hamilton has the same.

Sport loves an emotional link to records, so be prepared for this to become a big moment.

Five wins apiece for Michael and Lewis 🖐#F1 #ItalianGP pic.twitter.com/j10lMygYft.

The Italian team are bringing an upgrade engine to Monza for the weekend.

Hamilton would desperately love to go out at the top after what is a remarkable return to decent form after some years of desperate struggle.

With Antonelli possibly out of the running this weekend, this is the chance to change the - *spits in self-scorn* - narrative.

Russell might have incurred a penalty if he had done this in qualifying.

The Mercedes man blocked Oscar Piastri’s run at a corner, forcing some heavy braking from his rival.

Thankfully, Piastri ducked out, and thankfully for Russell, he’s not facing censure.

A near miss for Oscar Piastri! 😬 pic.twitter.com/y6UMu8wIDM.

The pair are just natural friends.

Industry observers note that max Verstappen and Lewis Hamilton go racing! 🍿 pic.twitter.com/Zs8u8h4XoT.

The former world champion is still looking for more from his car.

“Just looking at the deltas there, I was losing something like 0.6secs to George on the straights, which is something we need to look into,” Hamilton stated yesterday, before explaining his conundrum for qualifying, suggesting he may go out after Leclerc.

“The tow is everything here so [I’m] likely to be looking for the tow.”.

Because Antonelli exceeded the limit of parts used for his engine, he is taking a grid penalty at Monza.

Few would entirely rule out a storming ride for him on Sunday to end up top of the pack, but is is clearly a huge task for him to score points of any kind with that disadvantage.

They are now likely both past their peaks, but Hamilton and Verstappen recalled their battles of 2021 when they clashed in practice earlier.

Verstappen was already hacked off with Hamilton for seemingly obstructing his path earlier in the session, and they almost came together in the dying moments of the session.

Sources indicate that hamilton needed to take the escape road at the first chicane, where the pair made contact in 2021, as Verstappen looked to slip around his occasional rival. The two of them scarcely avoided another contact.

On the radios, Verstappen claimed, “He caused that,” while Hamilton reported to Ferrari that he was, “Blocked by Max.” Perhaps there will be more aggro later.

The full list of times from earlier today.

FP3 CLASSIFICATIONRussell in the box seat heading into qualifying#F1 #ItalianGP pic.twitter.com/BUrCsv92dT.

Welcome to Telegraph Sport’s live coverage of and qualifying for the Monza Grand Prix.

Before the weekend’s racing, George Russell was, at least publicly, less than bullish about his chances in Italy.

He did, though, believe he would deliver a better showing than he had in recent weeks.

“I don’t know if we can say we’re favourites this weekend, but we probably have a greater opportunity than we’ve had in the last two races where it’s been less about the power unit and more about the chassis,” he remarked.

In a recent development, “It’s so close right now, that last tenth in qualifying can be the difference of a couple of positions, which can change the podium. Right now, I don’t know who is going to be the team to beat.”.

Russell was almost a minute off winner Lando Norris of McLaren in Hungary, finishing seventh in his Mercedes. Two weeks ago, in the Netherlands, he took the last spot on the podium, with Norris winning again.

However, in the second practice session on Friday and FP3 today, Russell was quickest. He led his former colleague, Ferrari’s Lewis Hamilton, who was second fastest.

Red Bull’s Max Verstappen hinted at a rare good weekend as he was third fastest, about a third of a second behind Russell.

Russell, of course, needs a win soon, or he is in danger of seeing the championship run away from him entirely, as Kimi Antonelli already leads him by 59 points in the world title chase.

It has been revealed that perhaps psychologically just as pressing is that erstwhile teammate Hamilton is tied with Russell on 183 points, in third because he has one victory compared to Russell’s two. Slipping down the rankings could knock his confidence.

Russell has not secured pole for the last four races, so a strong showing in qualifying might be the boost he needs ahead of Sunday’s race, while Norris is looking for a pole position hat-trick.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, enzo Maresca ha rilasciato queste dichiarazioni nella conferenza stampa della vigilia dell sfida di Champions tra il suo Manchester City e il Napoli: “”Le parole di Allegri?
  • I Am Naples Testata Giornalistica - aut.

According to recent reports, enzo Maresca ha rilasciato queste dichiarazioni nella conferenza stampa della vigilia dell sfida di Champions tra il suo Manchester City e il Napoli: “”Le parole di Allegri? Credo che in Italia siamo abbastanza bravi a piangere, è una partita importante tre punti valgono per noi come per il Napoli, mi aspetto un Napoli come l’ho visto con il Torino. Problemi nostri difensivi e di equilibrio? Dobbiamo trovare quanto fatto nelle prime gare ufficiali, difensivamente abbiamo concesso poco, nel Napoli ho visto una squadra di giocatori forti, hanno top player come McTominay, Hojlund, Olivera, c’è anche Lang è in forma, sarà una partita difficile. Se ci sono stati contatti in primavera con il Napoli? Sono felicissimo di essere qua, ci sono stati contatti con squadre italiane, ma non con il Napoli. Il Napoli attende ma propone anche, ha giocatori offensivi forti, giocare contro una squadra italiana è sempre difficile. In futuro tornare in Italia? Mai dire mai. Cosa c’è da cambiare nel calcio italiano? Bisogna essere un po’ più coraggiosi. Il Napoli come lo vedo? Vedo una squadra che sta bene, crea tanto e ha singoli importanti. De Bruyne? Posso solo dire che è un ragazzo spettacolare, top, nessun dubbio che, se contento anche fuori dal calcio, darà una grossa mano al Napoli”.

Pocognoli's problems are just the tip of the iceberg when it comes to those running the show at the SFA

Published: 10:30 EST, 20 November 2026 | Updated: 11:25 EST, 20 November 2026.

For anyone with anything resembling a retentive memory, the alarm bells were going off all over the shop on the day Sebastien Pocognoli was unveiled as the fresh Scotland head coach.

Scottish Football Association (SFA) chief executive Ian Maxwell and chief football officer Craig Mulholland were there to crow about an extensive search of foreign fields to rival Captain Cook’s journeys around the Pacific and how data had helped land ‘one of Europe’s most sought-after coaches’ and secure the ‘aggressive, front-foot style of play’ that was going to bring a desired freshness.

In a recent development, it was impossible to avoid the elephant in the room, though. Two-and-a-half months earlier, ahead of the disaster zone that was the World Cup, they’d handed Steve Clarke a fresh four-year contract.

It has been revealed that he was the polar opposite to Poco. Aggressive and front-foot, he most certainly wasn’t. The SFA knew Clarke didn’t have it in him to go for it at a major finals – as evidenced by two separate European Championship failures – but they decided to stick with the status quo anyway. Just as they did after Euro 2024, when he should have been sacked.

When Clarke finally did go of his own accord after the summer’s events in North America, Maxwell stated he was ‘sad’ the former Kilmarnock manager had stepped down and put a big dollop of blame on ‘some fairly hysterical commentary back home’.

SFA chief football officer Craig Mulholland,  Pocognoli and SFA chief executive Ian Maxwell.

In a recent development, it just didn’t add up. How do you go from thinking a guy like Clarke is the future to tearing everything up, drafting in a London-based analytics firm to tell you who to go for as his replacement and coming up with a 39-year-old Belgian who wants to go for broke?

Industry observers note that ‘It doesn’t matter how you get there,’ offered Maxwell. ‘Let’s not get too hung up on the whys and the what-ifs.’.

Unfortunately, people are now starting to get hung up over the fact Pocognoli, for all the good on his CV, looks like he’s in the wrong movie – with his refusal to break from a failing three-at-the-back strategy suggesting a diploma from the Wilfried Nancy School of Intransigence ought to be on that resume too.

They are getting hung up on the fact captain Andy Robertson came out after the thrashing from Switzerland’s B-team to reveal the mood inside the camp has changed and warn there’s no breathing space to sort this out.

And they are getting hung up on the fact that it’s becoming considerably easier to reach the conclusion those above all of them at the very top of the SFA have never had a proper grip on things at all.

Clarke, of course, only exacerbated those concerns in September by expressing the view at a public event that Maxwell and Co ‘panicked a little bit’ in giving him that incomprehensible long-term deal because he’d threatened to announce he was quitting before the finals unless an agreement was reached.

Recent findings suggest that ‘I wanted to control my narrative,’ he explained. It was hard to know who emerged from those admissions looking worse.

Clarke’s off the plot now, though, and it’s Maxwell, Mulholland and the SFA president Mike Mulraney left to try and convince us all that there is some kind of rhyme or reason to it all.

Industry observers note that how things shape up with Pocognoli is an acid test for them. The rise or fall of a Scotland manager always hogs headlines. Yet, it is only one of a number of things coming together in what is starting to feel like a bit of a perfect storm.

Not so long ago, Maxwell and Mulholland were also yakking plenty about their statement project to increase game time for Scotland-eligible Under-21s.

In a recent development, it’s already in tatters, by the looks of things. The plans were watered down last month, without anything like the same fanfare, to involve Under-23 players and the intended votes on the proposals were pushed back.

A number of Premiership sides haven’t warmed to it and it remains to be seen whether it goes to a vote at all. Certainly, the radical change the top brass envisioned isn’t going to happen and that can only be regarded as an indicator that these guys running the game aren’t capable of taking it with them.

The start of Sebastien Pocognoli's reign has been concerning for Scotland fans.

Dundee manager Steven Pressley’s intervention over recent days hasn’t helped them either. After a long period on the outside looking in, Scotland have turned out in three major tournaments in the last five years.

Sources indicate that that has raised many millions of pounds, but the effect on elite level is questionable. Pressley talked of the sport being ‘built on sand’ as a result of there being no kind of national facility and you’d better believe it gained traction.

‘It indicates a lot about our strategy, our longevity and our long-term vision and we are finally seeing the effects of that. We have shown none of that over the period and it is all horribly catching up with us,’ he stated.

The SFA do own Hampden, of course, thanks to that peculiar £5million deal from 2019 that involved Willie Haughey and Sir Tom Hunter ponying up half the money. Yet, how distant those days of Maxwell talking about taking examples from the way VfB Stuttgart revamped the Mercedes-Benz Arena and potentially implementing them in Mount Florida seem now.

Everyone appears to have given up on making the National Stadium better. Other problems have overtaken that old chestnut. Refereeing isn’t good enough. VAR isn’t up to scratch. General facilities require considerable improvement.

Should this Youth Strategy fail, there may also be a need for the SFA to look deeper within when addressing the dearth of top-tier talent coming through.

In a recent development, it’s OK to blame clubs, but what about the level of coaching – and coach education – that exists at the national association? That’s before we even get to the ‘massive lack of expertise and education’ at the younger end of grassroots raised by St Mirren boss Craig McLeish.

The SFA set-up for producing coaches was once the envy of many. We all remember Jose Mourinho and others at the Largs finishing school. Now? Even Maxwell, after stating there were no viable Scottish rivals to Pocognoli for the Scotland job, admitted the coaching pathway needs looked at.

It has been revealed that there is only one problem here, though. Maxwell has been the chief executive since May 2018. He’s in his ninth year in the role. What has he really achieved? What have his big ideas been?

Yes, Scotland made it back to major finals under Clarke, but Clarke was a painfully obvious choice to be made national coach in 2019. He’d worked wonders at Rugby Park and did transfer that to the international scene until it came to actually turning out in those showpiece competitions.

Now they’ve had to get creative, there is so much hanging on Pocognoli’s reign for the guys at the top.

Recent findings suggest that maxwell was a bloke who landed in the role of Partick Thistle GM almost by mistake after failing to beat Jackie McNamara to the manager’s job. Just before leaving for the SFA, the Jags got relegated.

Talk of redeveloping Hampden has gone quiet as other problems take the spotlight.

At his Hampden unveiling, he had to fend off questions about only getting that position through behind-the-scenes politicking and insist he wouldn’t be a puppet for anyone.

Mulholland also seems a surprising choice as the architect of the national sport’s renovation. He spent two decades in the Rangers academy and eight years as head of it.

In a recent development, has it been a conveyor belt of talent for the Ibrox first-team? Do you recall much wailing and gnashing of teeth when he left in 2023 amid a wider changing of the guard?

Then, there’s Mulraney, the former Alloa chairman and SFA director for over a decade.

Recent findings suggest that you don’t see much of him these days. Maybe because people want to ask about his position as chair of FIFA’s finance committee in the wake of the most greed-infested World Cup ever and the ongoing soap opera surrounding Gianni Infantino. But maybe not.

How things work out with Pocognoli might end up being the one thing that puts all these guys under the kind of examination that cannot be bodyswerved, but it’s only the tip of the iceberg.

È l’immagine più dolorosa del weekend calcistico. Désiré Doué ha lasciato il campo in barella durante la sfida contro il Nizza dopo un contrasto fortuito, urlando di dolore. Gli esami successivi hanno confermato i timori: rottura del legamento crociato per il talento del Paris Saint-Germain, già costretto a fare i conti con l’assenza di Khvicha Kvaratskhelia per lo stesso tipo di problema.

Recent findings suggest that dopo i tanti messaggi di vicinanza ricevuti nelle ultime ore, il classe 2005 ha deciso di intervenire personalmente attraverso un messaggio pubblicato sui social. Il giovane francese ha espresso tutta la sua delusione, ma anche la volontà di reagire: "È un momento difficile. Questo infortunio mi rende triste. Ma sono convinto che tornerò molto più forte". Doué ha poi aggiunto: "Una nuova prova, una nuova occasione per crescere. Grazie a tutti per il sostegno e l’affetto che mi state dimostrando. Mantengo la fede".

It has been revealed that per l’esterno offensivo, arrivato al PSG dopo la crescita nel settore giovanile del Rennes, si apre ora una fase delicata della carriera. La rottura del crociato richiederà un lungo periodo di riabilitazione, con il club parigino chiamato a gestire un’altra pesante assenza nel reparto offensivo. Nonostante il momento difficile, Doué ha voluto trasmettere un messaggio di fiducia e determinazione: l’obiettivo è tornare in campo al meglio e dimostrare ancora una volta il proprio valore con la maglia del Paris Saint-Germain.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

This was the definition of a hard-earned point. Newcastle United came back from two goals down to rescue a point against Bournemouth, but this was not a convincing performance from Matthias Jaissle’s side.

Recent findings suggest that newcastle were abject for the first half an hour and the visitors could have been out of sight. It was disjointed and lacklustre as Bournemouth dominated before the break and regularly threatened Lukasz Hornicek in goal.

Even during the fightback, Newcastle lacked cohesion and penetration, but forced their way back into it through hard work, spirit and determination. Whether you believe Harvey Barnes’ wonder goal and Jacob Ramsey’s late strike paper over the cracks or reveal a togetherness – a grit and determination that bodes well for the future – depends on the individual.

According to recent reports, ramsey comes off the bench to fire Newcastle level! 🔥📺 Watch live on TNT Sports & HBO Max pic.twitter.com/UBWAfCQyy4.

Industry observers note that for the second weekend in a row, Newcastle had just two shots on target and scored two goals. At the other end of the pitch, they have allowed their opponents 61 shots in just three games, the highest in the division. That is not going to be sustainable long term. Something Jaissle acknowledged.

“It indicates where we have potential,” he noted. “There are elements to improve offensively.

“The learning curve is there. There were some elements missing from our performance but there was a strong response. The lads demonstrated significant character, big personality and big commitment... It is always better to get a point and see the potential to improve.”.

In a recent development, A reality check is not necessarily a bad thing. There has been a lot of hype and excitement on Tyneside and a self-congratulating tone to their own end of summer appraisals.

But this was a reminder of the team’s limitations and the fact that only three of their eight summer signings started the game, with two more coming off the bench, underlined they are a work in progress.

In a recent development, in truth, that is fine. It is the start of September and the Premier League campaign is only three games old. They have a new manager and a new-look team. There has been a significant amount of change in a very short period of time.

It was not the easiest summer, and despite the insistence from senior figures at the club that they had always remained calm and methodical during their summer reset, there was a whiff of crisis only a few weeks ago.

When Eddie Howe quit as manager and Bruno Guimarães, the captain, forced his move to Arsenal at the start of August, Newcastle looked in disarray. So, to have started the season unbeaten from three games against Liverpool, Tottenham Hotspur and Bournemouth is encouraging.

It is also worth highlighting just how good the visitors were. In the first half Bournemouth were superb, rushing Newcastle, forcing mistakes and pouring forward in numbers. In Alex Scott, just as he was in their victory here last season, Bournemouth had the best player on the pitch.

That opens up another conversation. Newcastle played like this a lot at home in Howe’s final season in charge, especially in the second-half of the campaign, but tended to lose not draw the game.

On this occasion, they secured a decent point with a late equaliser thanks to substitute Ramsey, who looked good when he replaced the off-colour Lewis Miley.

Bournemouth will feel they should have held on. They had taken a deserved lead through Marcus Tavernier, who took advantage of a static and ball-watching Amar Dedić to bundle home from close range.

Recent findings suggest that tavernier gives Bournemouth the lead at St James' Park! 🍒🔥📺 Watch live on TNT Sports & HBO Max pic.twitter.com/mDdb5uV4hj.

Marco Rose’s side should have scored again minutes later when Sven Botman gifted the ball to Evanilson on the edge of the Newcastle area, but he failed to hit the target.

Bournemouth had their tails up and when another blunder from Dedic – galloping forward and losing possession with a heavy touch – Nico González, another fresh signing, failed to make a tackle to stop the attack.

It has been revealed that justin Kluivert’s long-range strike thumped against the post and hit the back of goalkeeper Lukasz Hornicek. Scott reacted quickest and his cross spun into his own net off the leg of Malick Thiaw.

Bournemouth have a second and St James' Park is stunned! 😱📺 Watch live on TNT Sports & HBO Max pic.twitter.com/Kyy91awf39.

Newcastle were in disarray and were lucky to be back in the game before half-time as Barnes whipped in a stunning strike 25 seconds after the restart.

Bournemouth have a second and St James' Park is stunned! 😱📺 Watch live on TNT Sports & HBO Max pic.twitter.com/Kyy91awf39.

Despite seeing more of the ball, other than a Joe Willock header that dropped wide of the post early in the second half, Newcastle did not create another clear goal-scoring opportunity until Ramsey’s equaliser.

Industry observers note that that is a cause for concern, but Newcastle remain unbeaten. Nothing shapes perceptions more than results. Jaissle is right to cling to the positives from that.

Speaking to TNT Sports, the Newcastle boss noted: “Mixed feelings. Happy for that spirit, that belief the lads were showing until the end together with the crowd. I felt the energy and felt if we had five or 10 minutes more we could win this game. But the first half was not expected. This is something we need to improve. This is part of the journey.

Industry observers note that “We knew Bournemouth would come with everything, they always show great intensity and if you do not compete with that you get problems. We struggled with that in the first half but the lads revealed the right reaction.”.

Good morning and welcome to our live coverage of this Saturday lunchtime fixture between Newcastle United and Bournemouth at St James’ Park.

In a recent development, the hosts have made a determined start to the 2025-26 season under new head coach Matthias Jaissle. They conceded a last-minute penalty to draw 2-2 with Liverpool on the opening weekend of the Premier League campaign, sealed a hard-fought 3-2 victory over West Bromwich Albion in the Carabao Cup, and then produced an inspired second-half performance to win 2-0 away at Tottenham in their previous top-flight outing.

Despite anxiety in the summer after losing Eddie Howe and multiple key players such as Sandro Tonali, Bruno Guimaraes and Anthony Gordon, the Jaissle era has begun very encouragingly. Newly introduced signings including Lukas Hornicek, Amar Dedic and Nico Gonzalez have seamlessly slotted into the starting XI, Lewis Hall has been typically brilliant, while Anthony Elanga and Yoane Wissa look reborn up top after both forwards endured difficult campaigns last season.

Sources indicate that marco Rose’s Bournemouth tenure has started in frustrating circumstances. They had been leading 1-0 against Manchester City in their first top-flight fixture this campaign, but conceded two late goals to dramatically lose 2-1. Bournemouth were also left kicking themselves last weekend against Everton, after a defensive mix-up between Ryan Christie and Marcus Tavernier following a corner delivery gifted James Tarkowski a 91st-minute equaliser, allowing the visitors to salvage a 1-1 draw at the Vitality Stadium.

At opposite ends of the country, over 350 miles separate these two sides. Away days in English football can’t really get any longer. The travelling Bournemouth support will hope their loyalty can be repaid with a first Premier League win of the season under Rose, while Newcastle will aim to continue their unbeaten start and carry on the positive momentum created by Jaissle.

Kick-off is at 12:30, with team news coming shortly.

Tech Report: Flat-band-induced integer doping and phase transition in monolayer graphene

📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 44 min read (8826 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Nature

⏱️ ~44 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • van der Waals heterostructures are stabilized by a delicate balance between van der Waals, elastic and Coulomb energies1,2,3,4.
  • It has been revealed that unlike covalently bonded heterostructures, van der Waals heterostructures are stabilized by the delicate balance between van der Waals forces, Coulomb interactions and the local strain1,2,3,4.
  • The particular stacking configuration and the atomic registry between neighbouring layers are likewise controlled by the balance of those energies.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

van der Waals heterostructures are stabilized by a delicate balance between van der Waals, elastic and Coulomb energies1,2,3,4. Because the interfaces are not covalently bonded, the constituent crystals can slide, rotate and reconstruct, resulting in several possible competing structural phases2,5,6. However, controlled tuning of this balance, and hence dynamical control over the stacking, has yet to be achieved. Here we report a dynamical heterostructure in which monolayer graphene is doubly aligned to bulk hexagonal boron nitride (hBN) and monolayer hexagonal boron nitride (mhBN) on either side. In such a system, a global structural phase transition, manifested as a change of crystalline symmetry observed by scanning tunnelling microscopy, could be induced by gating, magnetic field or temperature. This structural transition is accompanied by an exotic electronic transition: the doping of graphene switches between discrete levels, corresponding to an exact integer number of electrons or holes per moiré plaquette. We attribute this integer doping to charge trapping in localized, strain-induced pseudo-Landau levels (flat bands in reciprocal space7,8,9,10,11,12), produced by moiré reconstruction (strongly enhanced by the mhBN). Electrical control of coupled structural and electronic phase transitions provides a route to engineering strain-induced flat bands and strain–Coulomb correlations in van der Waals heterostructures.

It has been revealed that unlike covalently bonded heterostructures, van der Waals heterostructures are stabilized by the delicate balance between van der Waals forces, Coulomb interactions and the local strain1,2,3,4. Depending on the relative weight of those energy terms, many different phenomena have been observed: the Hofstadter butterfly depending mainly on the van der Waals coupling13,14,15, commensurate–incommensurate phase transitions driven by van der Waals–strain competition5,6 and flat-band formation that probably involves all three contributions and facilitates superconductivity and correlated insulating phase 16,17,18.

The particular stacking configuration and the atomic registry between neighbouring layers are likewise controlled by the balance of those energies. Varying their relative contributions can switch the system between different atomic arrangements, resulting in structural phase transitions potentially accompanied by the emergence of fresh electronic phases. This points to a rich underlying phase diagram. Yet experimental platforms that allow controlled exploration of this phase space so far have been lacking.

Here we demonstrate that, by careful tuning of the balance between these competing interactions in a three-layer van der Waals heterostructure, we can reach simultaneous structural and electronic phase transitions, controlled through layer charging, magnetic field or temperature variation. We engineer these transitions in a heterostructure in which monolayer graphene is doubly aligned to bulk hBN and mhBN on either side: mhBN/graphene/hBN. In such heterostructures, strain is greatly enhanced because mhBN, unlike its bulk counterpart, is free to contract and corrugate (the strain amplitude is controlled by the number of hBN layers), leading to strongly enhanced surface reconstruction19,20,21. The van der Waals interaction of this system is likewise enhanced by the double alignment and can be tuned by gate-charging the graphene layer.

In such heterostructure devices, the structural phase transition reveals itself through an abrupt, global and reversible switch of the stacking configuration, which entails a change of symmetry (analogous to the Bernal-to-rhombohedral transition in graphite22,23,24,25) and results in distinct reconstruction modes observed directly by scanning tunnelling microscopy (STM). It is accompanied by a unique electronic phase transition: switching between p-doping and n-doping of graphene. Unlike conventional doping, the doping levels before and after the phase transition are discrete rather than continuous in nature, always taking an integer or ‘quantized’ value corresponding to an exact integer number of electrons per moiré unit cell, which we hereafter term integer doping. We attribute this integer doping to electrons (holes) being trapped in the strain-induced pseudo-Landau levels (PLLs), formed by the strong moiré surface reconstruction; these localized states constitute flat bands in k-space, as predicted theoretically7,8,9,10,11 and confirmed by STM measurements12. The structural transition alters the atomic arrangement, modifying both the strain and scalar-potential landscapes. In reciprocal space, we interpret this as switching the hybridization of these flat bands between the valence band (AB phase) and the conduction band (AA phase), inverting the sign of the integer doping.

Our heterostructure consists of monolayer graphene that is double-aligned, on one side to hBN and on the other side to mhBN (refs. 19,20). Unlike single alignment, such double-aligned ‘sandwich’ heterostructures can exhibit either parallel or antiparallel orientations corresponding to the 0° and 180° angle alignment between the top and bottom hBN (refs. 2,19,26). The results obtained on both types of device are similar, so in the main text, we focus on the parallel orientation, presenting the analysis for the antiparallel orientation in Supplementary Information Sections 20, 23, 26 and 28 (Supplementary Figs. 30, 41 and 42).

Sources indicate that for either orientation, two energetically competing stacking configurations exist (Fig. 1c,d), which are interconvertible by sliding the mhBN by one interatomic distance relative to the bulk hBN (detailed explanation and simple schematics in Supplementary Information Section 21; Supplementary Figs. 31 and 32). This is analogous to the transition between ABC (rhombohedral) and ABA (Bernal) trilayer graphene, in which a small shift of one of the layers leads to strong reconfigurations of the electronic bands22,23,24,25.

It has been revealed that a, Schematic representation of the full phase diagram formed in our double-aligned mhBN/graphene/hBN system. External parameters (such as carrier density n, magnetic field B and temperature T) define one coordinate axis, whereas the intrinsic stacking order of the sandwich heterostructure defines the other. Two local energy minima exist corresponding to AA and AB stacking configurations, with their dominant stackings shown in c and d, respectively. Blue and red arrows indicate transitions between these configurations; solid arrows denote states realized under continuous tuning of external parameters, whereas dashed arrows mark the abrupt structural phase transition, matching the solid and dashed lines in the experiments shown in Fig. 3a–c. b, Moiré-induced corrugation observed in a double-aligned mhBN/graphene/hBN device, measured at room temperature by AFM. Inset shows the corrugation profile along the light blue line. Phonon squeezing reduces corrugation at low temperatures. The unit cell outlined in black matches that in g. c,d, Schematic illustrations of the competing sandwich configurations at double-aligned interfaces: AB (c) and AA (d) stacking configurations. e–h, MD simulations of strain distributions. Panels g and h show our double-aligned mhBN/graphene/hBN configurations with AB and AA stacking configurations, respectively, and panels e and f show reference calculations for double-aligned hBN/graphene/hBN configurations. Comparison highlights the notable role of mhBN on strain enhancement, leading to much stronger reconstruction patterns—triangular and hexagonal reconstructions, respectively. Dashed circles indicate vertices of domains arising from these two reconstruction types, on which strain-induced PLLs develop, as shown on the right. The yellow-to-orange gradient bar indicates increasing strain amplitude. i, The theoretical calculated corrugation of the graphene–hBN interface as a function of the twist angle.

In a recent development, unlike previous studies that apply a mechanical tool such as an atomic force microscope or scanning tunnelling microscope tip to locally ‘iron’ the sample to toggle the stacking configurations in confined regions of sample27,28, our system allows global, reversible switching between the two stacking states simply by tuning external parameters, including carrier density n, magnetic field B or temperature T. Such all-electronic control is far better suited to device integration and to triggering newly introduced phenomena in transport measurements. The schematic in Fig. 1a illustrates the full phase diagram defined by these external parameters and the intrinsic stacking order, in which the two local minima correspond to the competing AB and AA stacking configurations. Accompanying this switch, the moiré-induced strain distribution and thus the lattice reconstruction changes from triangular to hexagonal patterns (Fig. 1e–h; see also the STM images in Fig. 5a,b), ultimately leading to different pseudomagnetic field (PMF) distributions2,29 (Fig. 5e,f) and different band reconfigurations (Fig. 5g–j).

We emphasize that the mhBN is essential for enhancing such lattice reconstruction of graphene, as mhBN itself can accommodate a finite amount of strain, allowing both layers (mhBN and graphene) to undergo very strong relaxation. The molecular dynamics (MD) simulations, comparing mhBN/graphene/hBN (Fig. 1g,h) and hBN/graphene/hBN (Fig. 1e,f) heterostructures, clearly demonstrate that the presence of mhBN greatly amplifies the periodic strain induced by moiré reconstruction. The experimental evidence, including room-temperature atomic force microscopy (AFM) measurement of the corrugation (Fig. 1b) and the same measurement with varying hBN layer numbers (1–4 layers; Supplementary Information Section 13; Supplementary Fig. 19) and their corresponding transport properties, is presented in Supplementary Information Section 4. As well as mhBN, alignment also markedly influences the strain, as shown by the calculated corrugation with respect to the twist angle in Fig. 1i.

Two types of transport device are discussed in the main text: dual-gated hBN/graphene/mhBN/hBN (Fig. 2a) and bottom-gated mhBN/graphene/hBN (Fig. 2b). In the former, the mhBN–hBN interface is intentionally misaligned by 15° to achieve superlubricity, preserving the double-aligned sandwich structure. The two architectures are complementary: the dual-gated capped devices enable higher carrier concentrations and allow the roles of doping and the displacement field to be disentangled (Supplementary Information Section 8), whereas the non-capped mhBN/graphene/hBN structure develops stronger reconstruction, in particular the out-of-plane corrugation at the graphene–mhBN interface (Supplementary Information Section 30).

a, Schematic of the transport device with hBN/graphene/mhBN/hBN heterostructure (inset) in a dual-graphite gate configuration. b, Schematic of the mhBN/graphene/hBN transport device. The unencapsulated mhBN enables AFM measurement. Inset, AFM image of the device (bottom right) and its fast Fourier transform (FFT). The FFT confirms the double alignment and gives the periods of both superlattices, which agree well with those derived from the transport measurement in d. Scale bar, 50 nm. c,d, Longitudinal resistance Rxx of the states before (blue) and after (red) the transition in the device types in a and b, measured at T = 1.6 K. The neutrality point, labelled ‘NP’, shifts from no doping to n-doping (device in a) and from p-doping to n-doping (device in b) on transition. The top axis marks doping levels corresponding to integer multiples of electrons or holes per moiré unit cell. The doping shift relative to zero is denoted by Δnint, in which ‘int’ signifies intrinsic doping (in contrast to external doping by gate). For the device in a, the bottom axis (Vdual D = 0) is defined such that both Vtg and Vbg are simultaneously tuned to vary carrier density while maintaining zero displacement field in graphene. By contrast, the device in b has only back gate, so its bottom axis is represented by Vbg. e,f, The doping levels of other same-structured devices with different periods of moiré plaquette λm before (blue dots) and after (red dots) transition. The details of all samples are presented in Supplementary Information Section 3 and Supplementary Figs. 5 and 6. The doping levels of all samples, before and after the transition, are located at integer multiples of electrons per moiré unit cell, with the percentage deviation from ideal integer multiples (Δnint − Nn0)/Nn0 shown by bar graphs at the corresponding positions, in which Δnint − Nn0 is the deviation from the nearest integer multiple N (if N is 0, then we choose the denominator Nn0 = n0).

It has been revealed that for both architectures, double alignment of graphene to the hBN crystals on both sides was confirmed by AFM, Raman and transport measurements (Methods; Supplementary Information Section 2). We emphasize that both the double alignment and the presence of mhBN are crucial for the effects we observe, as corroborated by seven types of reference device, none of which exhibit the transition (Methods; Supplementary Information Section 4; Supplementary Figs. 7 and 8).

In a recent development, first, let us examine the initial-state transfer curves (blue) of the two device types in Fig. 2c,d. In the hBN/graphene/mhBN/hBN sample, the neutrality point of graphene remains at zero doping, whereas the mhBN/graphene/hBN structure exhibits p-doping. Notably, this p-doping level closely approximates 2n0 (n0 corresponds to doping of one charge carrier per moiré plaquette). In 8 of 9 unencapsulated mhBN/graphene/hBN devices (blue dots in Fig. 2f), the p-doping is quantized at Nn0 (N is an integer between 1 and 4), growing with the moiré period but always fixed at integer multiples of n0.

In Fig. 2e,f, the moiré period, determined from the carrier density of secondary Dirac points, exceeds in many samples the rigid-lattice limit of 14 nm (set by the 1.8% graphene–hBN lattice mismatch) and even reaches 17.7 nm, a consequence of the strain enhancement by mhBN and double alignment19,20 (Methods; Supplementary Information Section 4).

Sources indicate that by applying a large positive gate voltage above a certain threshold, a phase transition can be initiated: the moiré period remains unchanged but the samples become n-doped, again by an integer number of electrons per moiré plaquette, for both bottom-gated and dual-gated samples (Fig. 2c,d), and consistently across samples with different moiré sizes (Fig. 2e,f; Supplementary Information Section 3; Supplementary Figs. 5 and 6). Comprehensive control experiments (Supplementary Information Sections 5 and 14; Supplementary Figs. 9–11 and 20–22) verify that this transition and the integer doping are intrinsic, excluding artefacts such as contamination. We emphasize that the integer doping is a direct observation requiring no fitting or registration procedure. As is well established for graphene superlattices5,6,7, the neutrality point–secondary Dirac point separation is fixed at four electrons per moiré unit cell. In Fig. 2c, the post-transition neutrality point (red) falls precisely at the midpoint between the pre-transition neutrality point and the secondary Dirac point (blue) and hence corresponds to exactly two electrons per moiré unit cell, as highlighted by the equally spaced ruler.

Industry observers note that note that for the dual-gated samples (Fig. 2c), the gate voltage was applied simultaneously through top and bottom gates along the D = 0 line30 (dashed line in Fig. 3a). The switching depends only on the total carrier concentration and not on the displacement field (Supplementary Information Section 8; Supplementary Fig. 14). This mechanism fundamentally differs from recently reported two-dimensional ferroelectric systems, in which transitions occur through external electric-field-induced polarization changes26,31,32.

In a recent development, a–c, Vtg–Vbg maps of the transition process, each obtained by sweeping Vbg at stepped Vtg; a–c differ in gate sweep range and sweep history (marked by orange arrows). Numbers for blue lines and arrows give the doping per moiré unit cell at neutrality point (NP, 0), secondary Dirac points (SDP, ±4), tertiary Dirac points (TDP, ±8) and quaternary Dirac points (QDP, ±12); numbers for red lines and arrows are the same points offset by −2 electrons. Dashed lines indicate abrupt state changes at transition. The dashed black line in a denotes zero displacement field (D = 0), along which all transfer curves in Figs. 2 and 3 were performed; all forward and reverse transitions in a–c occur on this line, indicating that the displacement field is not the driving mechanism. In a–c, the transition point and the post-transition state are independent of gate range and sweep history. d, Continuous monitoring of the transition. Blue and red solid lines are states before and after transition, respectively. Notably, transition occurs at 3.8 T, at which magnetic length (approximately 13.4 nm) becomes commensurate with moiré periodicity. f,g, Zoom-in views of the blue and red boxed regions in d, respectively, revealing abrupt state changes at critical voltages (dashed lines). Circles represent the plotted resistance points; arrows indicate transition-induced resistance jump. h, Correlation between Rxx and Rxy; top axis, measured Hall density nfree; bottom axis, total gate-induced charge ntotal. The Hall zero-crossing (nfree = 0) occurs at ntotal = 2 holes per moiré cell, the difference being the localized charge nloc.

To investigate the transition dynamics and reproducibility, we conducted a series of Vtg–Vbg mappings and repeated switching tests (Rxx in Fig. 3; Rxy in Supplementary Fig. 24). Figure 3a–c reveals several Dirac points separated by intervals of four electrons per moiré plaquette5,6,7, marked with blue (before transition) or red (after transition) lines or arrows.

According to recent reports, the phase transition occurs at Vtg = +3.9 V, Vbg = +5.3 V corresponding to ntotal = 3.75 × 1012 cm−2 along the D = 0 line in Fig. 3a. Following the transition, all features shift by two electrons per moiré plaquette. This shift throughout the entire superlattice spectrum clearly indicates that the moiré period is unchanged. The recovery occurs at Vtg = −5.0 V, Vbg = −6.9 V (corresponding to −4.85 × 1012 cm−2), also along the D = 0 line, restoring the entire gate dependence (Fig. 3b). Comparing Fig. 3c with Fig. 3a shows that different Vtg–Vbg ranges and sweep protocols do not affect the transition characteristics: it occurs at identical gate points, as a single discrete event at the critical voltage rather than a continuous evolution.

Figure 3d illustrates the transition dynamics through sequential measurements (swp1–swp8), with dashed lines at +5.3 V and −6.9 V marking the critical voltages for the forward and reverse transitions, respectively. Below the critical voltage, no transition occurs (swp1–swp2); on reaching it, the transition happens (swp3–swp4), at a critical voltage independent of the gate sweep rate (Supplementary Information Section 15; Supplementary Fig. 23). Similar behaviour is observed for the reverse transition (steps swp4–swp7). Figure 3f,g reveals zoomed-in views around the critical voltages for both the forward and reverse transitions. At the moment of transition, the resistance jumps from one state to another without any intermediate states, consistent with the abrupt translation of features observed in Vtg–Vbg mappings of Fig. 3a–c. Once the transition is induced, further increasing the gate voltage yields no continuous effect, indicating a saturation mechanism defined by the moiré unit cell capacity rather than the strength of the applied field. This behaviour differs markedly from that of ferroelectrics, for which polarization scales continuously with the applied field. The switching is fully reproducible: 100 consecutive cycles yield curves that overlap precisely (Fig. 3d, top). All behaviours discussed above support that the observed phase transition is a first-order-like transition (further information in Supplementary Information Section 43).

Notably, the transition can also be controlled by the magnetic field. Mapping the transition from 13 T down to 0 T (Fig. 3e) reveals that the transition is suppressed at high field, even for gate voltages far exceeding the critical value, and reappears at exactly the same critical voltage once the field drops below Bcrit = 3.8 T. The origin of this suppression remains to be established; we note, however, that the magnetic length at critical field \(\sqrt{\hbar /e{B}_{{\rm{crit}}}}\approx 13.4\,{\rm{nm}}\) is comparable with the moiré period for this sample of 13.8 nm.

In a recent development, in Fig. 3h, correlating Rxx with Rxy gives further information for theoretical analysis: the Hall-resistivity zero crossing (zero free carrier density nfree) occurs at a gate-induced density of two holes per moiré unit cell, the difference being compensated by localized electrons nloc.

To identify the origin of the phase transition, we consider the balance between elastic (strain) and van der Waals forces5,6, which can be modified through Coulomb interactions introduced by gate charging the graphene layer.

Using high-throughput density functional theory (DFT), we calculated the adhesion-energy distribution across the non-relaxed moiré plaquette, assuming perfect alignment of hBN on both sides, for the AB (Fig. 4a) and AA (Fig. 4b) relative configurations of the two hBN crystals (Supplementary Information Section 22; Supplementary Figs. 33–35). The relative energy of the two configurations can be compared by averaging the van der Waals potential over the entire moiré unit cell, as illustrated in Fig. 4c. The AB structure exhibits lower energy under neutral charging conditions (Fig. 4c–e). However, by assigning a negative charge on graphene above a certain threshold (corresponding to positive gate voltage applied) the AA configuration becomes more energetically favourable than AB (Fig. 4c,f,g), resulting in a structural phase transition from AB to AA.

Industry observers note that a,b, Schematics of the two configurations (AB (a) and AA (b)) and three high-symmetry stacking sites for both configurations. The red arrows on the left side indicate a shift of one of the hBN layers by one interatomic distance. c, Schematic diagram of the relative stability (in terms of the average adhesion energy taken over the entire moiré plaquette) of the two configurations as a function of doping. The solid lines represent the energy-favourable state. The crossing of the blue and red lines indicates the occurrence of the transition. Electron doping (positive gate) switches the relative stability between the two configurations and the consequent modification of the interlayer adhesion is proposed to be the driving force. d–g, Distribution of the interlayer adhesion energy (Eadh) across the moiré plaquette for the AB (d,f) and AA (e,g) configurations in the case of zero (d,e) and n-type (f,g) external doping (induced by gating in our experiments). The graphs in the middle give the corresponding adhesion energies of the three high-symmetry stackings as a function of interlayer distance between graphene and the top and bottom boron nitride layers near the equilibrium spacing (2.7–4.0 Å).

The energy evolution with doping arises from gate-introduced Coulomb interactions, which enter the competition between van der Waals forces and elastic energies5,6. The balance among these three factors can be understood by comparing the relative stability of the AB and AA stacking configurations at high-symmetry points (Fig. 4a,b), which are the most representative sites and capture the qualitative trends under gating. Specifically, n-type doping substantially reduces the interlayer potential of AA-3 stacking: there, carbon atoms are vertically aligned with boron and the added electrons on carbon are strongly attracted to the positive charge on boron arising from the ionic nature of B–N bonds33. By contrast, the interlayer potential of AA-2 stacking is slightly elevated by the repulsion between the added electrons and the negatively charged nitrogen, whereas AA-1 and all three high-symmetry sites of the AB alignment remain almost unchanged, as the interaction of added electrons with boron is compensated by their interaction with nitrogen. This picture is substantiated by DFT calculations (Fig. 4d–g; Supplementary Information Sections 22–27). We can generalize the similar gate-induced phase transitions to other systems in which at least one of the multiply aligned layers has electropolarity (Supplementary Information Section 37).

It has been revealed that we now turn to the origin of the integer doping in graphene, which we attribute to strain-induced PLLs localized at the vertices of the reconstructed moiré domains. The reconstructed phases for AB and AA configurations are directly visualized through STM measurements (STM images of different regions, and of a reference single-aligned graphene/hBN region on the same flake, are shown in Supplementary Figs. 12 and 13) and theoretically simulated by MD calculations (Fig. 5a,b). On the basis of the atomic displacements calculated by MD, we obtained the strain distribution in the reconstructed moiré unit cell (schematics shown in Fig. 5c,d), as well as the associated pseudomagnetic field7,8,9,10,11,34 (left panels of Fig. 5e,f) (Supplementary Information Sections 24, 29 and 31).

It has been revealed that the reconstruction results in distinct strain fields for the AB and AA configurations (Fig. 5c,d). For the AB configuration, it is the AB-1 and AB-3 stackings that have much lower energy than AB-2 (Fig. 4d,f), so the reconstruction forms triangular domains of AB-1 and AB-3 stackings, accompanied by notable strain and out-of-plane corrugation at the AB-2 stacking (Fig. 5c). By contrast, for the AA configuration, it is the AA-3 stacking that has the lowest energy (Fig. 4e,g), leading to hexagonally reconstructed AA-3 moiré domain, with the strain concentrated at AA-2 and AA-1 stacked corners of the moiré plaquette (Fig. 5d). Here the predominance of in-plane strain in AA (versus out-of-plane corrugation in AB) originates from the mirror symmetry of the AA configuration, which yields negligible net out-of-plane force (Supplementary Information Section 38; Supplementary Fig. 54). In both cases, the strain results in strong PMF.
